newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Giddings-Thyssen match strong, faces hurdles.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Giddings-Thyssen match strong, faces hurdles.

text.p: Giddings & Lewis Inc's agreement to be acquired for $21 per share by Thyssen AG looks likely to proceed, although obstacles could emerge from the U.S. Defense Department or a rival bidder.
Harnischfeger Industries Inc, which has pursued Fond du Lac, Wis.-based Giddings since late April, is unlikely to raise its $19-per-share tender offer, analysts said.
"Harnischfeger has shown remarkable discipline. It's not a high probablility that HPH will come back. But it's not impossible," said Schroder Wertheim analyst Eli Lustgarten.
Milwaukee-based Harnischfeger said Thursday morning it was reviewing the Thyssen-Giddings announcement, but would not comment until later in the day.
The chance that another would-be acquirer might step up appeared equally remote, although analysts had said the same thing before Thyssen came into the picture.
"I wouldn't hold my breath on more people coming out of the woodwork. But you never say 'never'," Lustgarten said.
The deal could face federal government scrutiny because Thyssen is a German company and Giddings is involved in the militarily critical machine tool business, analysts said.

"Giddings & Lewis has some very important proprietary technology ... So that's an issue. Anti-trust (issues) I don't think can be shrugged off, either," said Chicago Corp analyst Robert McCarthy. "I don't think it's likely that either issue would block the deal, but they are potential obstacles."
In early over-the-counter trading, Giddings shares rose 2 to the Thyssen offer of 21, while Harnischfeger was up 1 to 41-3/4 in New York Stock Exchange morning action.
In a statement, Giddings said the Thyssen deal was "in the best interests of all ... constituencies." The firm said it will retain its name, headquarters and management team.

"I don't know why Giddings wants to sell to a German company, rather than another Wisconsin-based company. Two dollars more doesn't seem like that much. I hope this isn't just all about management wanting to keep their jobs," said Barrington Research analyst Walter Liptak.

In the company's statement, Giddings chairman Marvin Isles said, "Backed by Thyssen's financial strength and global resources, Giddings & Lewis is strategically positioned to focus on our core purpose -- providing customers worldwide with the products and services they need to improve their manufacturing productivity."
He added, "Thyssen is the right partner for Giddings & Lewis. We are like-minded about how to achieve our goals."

Giddings, which makes automation products and machine tools, reported 1996 revenues of $763 million. Based in Duesseldorf, Thyssen has annual revenues of about $26.2 billion and owns 320 companies worldwide in a wide variety of industries.
Harnischfeger makes heavy machinery and manufacturing systems for papermaking, mining and materials handling. Its 1996 revenues were about $2.9 billion.

Harnischfeger unveiled its bid for Giddings six weeks ago. At that time, the aggregate value of the deal was about $747 million, including $116 million in debt assumption. The bid was rejected as inadequate on May 8 by the Giddings board, but Harnischfeger said it would appeal to shareholders.
In recent days, Giddings and Harnischfeger have squabbled over the setting of a date for a special shareholders meeting to consider the Harnischfeger offer.
